idiom_name: Array.prototype.filter with a type-predicate criterion (value is S) so the filtered array is narrowed
implementation_notes: The JavaScript method is the mechanism and TypeScript's contribution is the type-level one: the library overload filter<S extends T>(predicate: (value: T, index: number, array: T[]) => value is S): S[] lets a criterion carry a claim about the element type, so fish.filter(isFish) is Fish[] rather than (Fish | Bird)[], and since TypeScript 5.5 the checker infers type predicates for eligible one-line predicates such as t => t !== undefined. Criteria therefore compose as named, reusable guards - the pattern's 'criteria are first-class' claim enforced by the compiler. A container-typed filtered copy is a class method returning new ThreatAwareSystem(this.systemId, this.threats.filter(keep)), and iterator helpers are typed the same way for lazy chains; runtime-only criteria need no type predicate, they just keep the plain boolean overload.
pitfalls: Narrowing is lost as soon as the criterion stops being a type predicate: wrapping it ((t) => isRootkit(t)), inlining a truthiness check, or filter(Boolean) - and filter(Boolean)/filter(x => !!x) also drops legitimate falsy values such as 0 and ''.

The 5.5 inference rules are strict (no explicit return type, a single return, no parameter mutation), so refactoring a predicate into a multi-statement body silently reverts the result to the wide element type.
A type predicate is a claim, not a check: if the runtime test is wrong the compiler trusts it and every downstream use is unsound, because 'is' is not re-verified against the implementation.
filter on ReadonlyArray returns a mutable S[], and the callback's index/array parameters leak when a predicate is passed by name (same trap as plain JavaScript, now typed as accepting them).
